title: A nonproper connected group contains a positive-dimensional affine subgroup
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Group schemes and homomorphisms are as in [def-sc-group-scheme], closed and normal subgroups as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], smoothness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme], and finite type as in [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Affine means isomorphic to the spectrum of a commutative ring [def-pc-scheme]. Dimensions are topological Krull dimensions [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Let $H$ be a smooth connected separated finite-type $k$-group scheme which is not proper over $k$. There exists a smooth connected affine closed subgroup scheme $U\hookrightarrow H$ with $\dim U>0$. The subgroup $U$ is not asserted to be normal in $H$. No commutativity assumption is imposed on $H$.

source.place: Proposition 8.25 (Rosenlicht dichotomy), printed pp.153--154. Passing from its positive-dimensional affine subgroup to its reduced identity component uses Corollary 1.35 and Corollary 1.39, printed pp.17--18. No equivariant-completion theorem is assumed: the source notes that its later Theorem 8.44 uses Proposition 8.25. No Stacks tag states this dichotomy.

proof.text: Write $G$ for the group called $H$ in the statement. Prove the assertion for all such groups by strong induction on $d=\dim G$. The dimension clause of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-subgroup-products] makes $d$ a finite nonnegative integer, bounds dimensions of closed subgroups, and gives strict dimension drop for proper smooth connected subgroup inclusions. If $d=0$, [lem-pc-zero-dimensional-closed-subscheme-finite] applied to the identity closed immersion $G\hookrightarrow G$ makes $G$ finite over $k$, hence proper by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-proper], a contradiction. Thus $d>0$.

source.place: Proposition 8.25, pp.153--154; dimension induction in the referenced Milne (2013), Proposition 4.1 proof. Zero-dimensional case: Stacks Tag 06LH, varieties.tex, lemma-algebraic-scheme-dim-0 (as recorded in the cited finite-scheme node).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-rational-boundary-positive-stabilizer] to obtain $X,P,V,\alpha$ and the reduced closed subgroup $S$ with $\dim S\geq1$. Let $C=(S^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], $C$ is a smooth connected integral separated finite-type closed subgroup. By [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], the finitely many components of $S$ are translates of $S^0$ and thus have the same dimension. A chain of irreducible closed subsets in a finite disjoint union of open-and-closed components lies in a single component. Consequently $\dim S=\dim S^0=\dim C$, the last equality because reduction leaves the topological space unchanged. In particular $\dim C>0$.

source.place: Proposition 8.25, p.154, rational-action paragraph; Corollaries 1.35 and 1.39 and dimension discussion, pp.17--18. Identity subgroup and smooth reduction: Stacks 0B7R, 047R, 047P/047N.

proof.text: First suppose $C=G$. Then $S=G$, so the partial stabilizer is Zariski dense in $G$. In the open $V$, the equalizer of $g\mapsto\alpha(g,P)$ and $g\mapsto P$ is closed (pull back the closed diagonal of $X$) and contains that dense set. Its defining ideal is zero: on each affine open of $V$, which is reduced by smoothness of $G$ and [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced],, every element of the ideal lies in every prime, hence is nilpotent and therefore zero. Thus $\alpha$ fixes $P$ on $V$. Its regular action on the dense open $j(G)$ is faithful: if a subgroup acts trivially, evaluation at $j(e)$ makes its inclusion in $G$ the identity section, on all algebra points. Apply [lem-sfb-rational-fixed-point-affineness] to obtain that $G$ is affine. Taking $U=G$ proves this case, since $d>0$.

source.place: Proposition 8.25 rational-action proof; Proposition 8.9 finite-jet argument, p.150; final case of the referenced Milne (2013), Proposition 4.1 proof, p.9.

proof.text: Henceforth $C\neq G$, so $\dim C<d$ by the strict dimension clause of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-subgroup-products]. If $C$ is not proper, the induction hypothesis applies to $C$ and gives a smooth connected affine closed subgroup $U\hookrightarrow C$ with positive dimension. Its composite into $G$ is closed: locally the composite of the two quotient maps of coordinate rings is a quotient map. It has all the required properties, so this case is complete.

source.place: Proposition 8.25, p.154, rational-action proof; proper-stabilizer induction in Milne (2013), Proposition 4.1 proof, p.8.

proof.text: It remains that $C$ is proper. It is an abelian variety by [def-sc-abelian-variety]. By [lem-sfb-abelian-subvariety-central], its inclusion in $G$ is central. Apply [lem-sfb-rosenlicht-connected-almost-complement] to $C\hookrightarrow G$. Obtain a smooth connected separated finite-type closed normal subgroup $N\hookrightarrow G$ and a surjective faithfully flat homomorphism $m:C\times_kN\to G$ with $\dim G=\dim C+\dim N$. Since $\dim C>0$, this gives $\dim N<d$.

source.place: Corollary 8.13, p.151; Theorem 8.24, p.153; complete-stabilizer case in the referenced Milne (2013), Proposition 4.1 proof, pp.8--9.

proof.text: The group $N$ cannot be proper. Otherwise $C\times_kN$ is proper: its projection to $N$ is the base change of the proper structure map of $C$ by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-base-change], and compose with the proper structure map of $N$ by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-composition]. By [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-theoretic-image-proper], its scheme-theoretic image under $m$ in the separated finite-type $G$ is proper. This image is all of $G$: surjectivity gives its full underlying space, and $G$ is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. On an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}B$ the image ideal lies in every prime of $B$, hence is zero since $B$ is reduced. This would make $G$ proper, contradicting the hypothesis. Apply the induction hypothesis to the nonproper $N$, whose dimension is smaller, obtaining the desired smooth connected affine positive-dimensional $U\hookrightarrow N$. Compose its closed inclusion with $N\hookrightarrow G$ as in step 4. This completes the induction and proves the statement without asserting normality of $U$ in $G$.

source.place: Proposition 8.25 rational-action proof; complete-stabilizer almost-complement case in Milne (2013), Proposition 4.1 proof, pp.8--9. Proper image: Stacks Tag 0AH6, morphisms.tex, lemma-scheme-theoretic-image-is-proper; Milne Appendix A.75(c),(d).

The statement is unchanged, and this is a first split, not a 2026-10-21 re-split. The strong induction on dim G holds. Base case: zero-dimensional implies finite, hence proper. Step 2 takes C=(S^0)_red with dim C=dim S>=1, via the component-translates and identity-component nodes. In step 3 (C=G) the equalizer argument on reduced V and faithfulness by evaluation at j(e) meet every hypothesis of rational-fixed-point-affineness. In step 4 (C not proper) the strict dimension drop allows induction. In step 5 (C proper) C is an abelian variety, the new centrality node applies, and then the existing almost-complement node. In step 6 a proper N would make the scheme-theoretic image of C x N, which is all of reduced G, proper, a contradiction; so induction applies to N. I checked the new nodes myself because Milne 2013 is not held locally. Boundary node: the orbit of the boundary point stays in the boundary, so the stabilizer has dimension at least dim G - dim boundary >= 1. If (g,P) and (h,gP) lie in Dom then (hg,P) does, so the partial stabilizer is a constructible submonoid and its closure is a subgroup. Tested on Ga and Gm in P^1, E x Ga, and Ga^2.
